title: Antimatter Drop
hook: Drop antimatter. See which way it falls.
sub: Tilt a magnetic trap the way CERN's ALPHA-g experiment did (Nature, 2023), open it, and count where the antihydrogen escapes. Every atom's fate is rolled with the paper's own odds, using random bits measured on all 156 qubits of IBM's ibm_fez.
you_control: Set the magnetic bias (11 settings from -3 g to +3 g, plus the +/-10 g calibration)
Stack antihydrogen: one trial or a full series, sized from the paper's Table 1
Ramp the mirror coils down: drag the one-way slider or press Ramp, pause any time, switch the dice source mid-ramp

Read where your atoms balance (the antihydrogen host walks to your fit) and, under The data, the escape curve and the |B| sketch; overlay the 1-D 'other worlds', run the whole campaign, hear each die land (optional sound with mute), take the quiz
qubits_note: comet-qrng-v1 on ibm_fez: 148 register + 8 Bell-witness = 156 qubits, reported by the job's provenance.circuit (n_rand 148, n_total 156); initial_layout covers physical qubits 0-155, the whole chip. Emulator bank at the 20-qubit emu cap (20 + 0).
honesty: The physics is Table 1 of Anderson et al., Nature 621, 716-722 (2023) (background-corrected, not efficiency-corrected, nominal biases); the only quantum step is the dice: 110,710 conditioned bytes from all 156 qubits of ibm_fez (entropy-accounted under the engine's stated pairwise-independence assumption, CHSH S = 2.548 +/- 0.015 as a fidelity witness, not device-independent certification), with an Aer emulator bank and the browser's classical RNG as interchangeable alternatives; timing, motion, tracks, the logistic balance-point fit and the 'other worlds' are classical cartoons, not the paper's 3-D analysis.
